title: [Chapitre] III. Réseaux via découpages : notes manuscrites (08/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Chapter III of the 1986 notes, 'Réseaux via découpages'. On the previous page Grothendieck worked concretely on the real line L. There he listed its 'tronçons': closed segments [s,t], half-lines ]-inf,s] and [s,+inf[, and the whole line. He gave their boundaries ({s,t}, {s}, the empty set) and defined a 'position' as a finite disjoint union of tronçons whose boundaries are mutually in that position. On this page he abstracts the order-theoretic content. He first drafts a heading, 'Définition: Segments, intervalles, demi-intervalles (cas d'une structure de réseau)', crosses it out and replaces it with 'tronçons'. On the next page the term becomes 'tranchée'.

Definition: a (partially) ordered set L is a 'tronçon ordonné' if:
(a) for every a in L with L_{>a} nonempty, L_{>a} is down-directed. That is, if x>a and y>a there is z with x,y >= z > a. Elements above a cannot 'fork' near a.
(a') The dual axiom: if x<a and y<a there is z with x,y <= z < a.
(b) L is directed both upward and downward: any x,y have a common lower bound a and a common upper bound b.
(c) If x<y there is z with x<z<=y.
(d) card L > 1. The marginal NB explains why (d) is needed: the other axioms hold trivially when card L <= 1.

The page then begins a classification. L is a 'segment' if it has both a least and a greatest element, and an 'intervalle' if it has neither. Page 9 adds 'demi-intervalle' for exactly one of the two, the boundary ∂L (the set of extremal elements), and self-duality under order reversal.

Purpose: an axiomatic, purely order-theoretic 'line' or 'interval' notion. Its boundary and its flag complex will serve as building blocks for the combinatorial 'réseaux' and 'découpages'. Page 9 defines Drap_2(L) as the comparable pairs and Drap(L) as the finite chains, i.e. the order complex. This is the combinatorial-topology side of the 'tame topology' programme of the Esquisse.
errors: Axiom (c) as written is vacuous: z = y always works. Grothendieck probably intended a non-trivial condition, e.g. density (x<z<y), existence of an element between x and y comparable to both, or some local finiteness or covering condition. As it stands it imposes nothing.

If L is totally ordered, axioms (a), (a') and (b) are automatic for nonempty L, so the definition reduces to 'a totally ordered set with at least 2 elements'. The axioms only have content if 'ensemble ordonné' means partially ordered. Yet page 9's formula Drap_2(L) = {{x,y} | x<y} and the trichotomy statement read most naturally for total orders. The intended generality (poset vs. chain) is left ambiguous.

The trichotomy segment / intervalle / demi-intervalle actually has four cases (both extremes, neither, only a min, only a max). It is correct once both one-sided cases are grouped as 'demi-intervalles', as page 9 does.

ideas.what: Axiomatic order-theoretic notion of a 'line piece' (tronçon/tranchée): an ordered set with local directedness above and below each point, global up/down directedness, and at least 2 elements
ideas.modern_name: abstract interval / linearly ordered space; directed poset with local directedness
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical order theory (Hausdorff, Cantor); no single attribution

ideas.what: Classification of such ordered pieces into segments, intervals and half-intervals by existence of least/greatest elements, with boundary ∂L = the extremal elements and self-duality under order reversal
ideas.modern_name: closed/open/half-open intervals of an ordered set; boundary of a 1-cell

ideas.what: Use of these pieces and their boundaries as building blocks for combinatorial 'réseaux'/'découpages' (tame, piecewise-linear dissection structures), leading on page 9 to the flag (order) complex Drap(L)
ideas.modern_name: order complex / nerve of a poset; cell decompositions in o-minimal or tame topology
ideas.usually_credited_to: order complex: P. Alexandroff, later Quillen/Björner; tame topology: van den Dries and others
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) sketches 'topologie modérée' only programmatically

missed.claim: Axiom (c) is vacuous as written; the intended non-trivial axiom (density or a covering/finiteness condition) was never fixed on this page. The partial-order vs. total-order generality is also left unresolved.
missed.quote: c) Si x, y ∈ L tels que x < y, ∃ z tel que x < z ≤ y
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor. It only matters for anyone reconstructing the exact axiomatics of Grothendieck's 1986 combinatorial 'réseaux', which are part of his unpublished tame-topology material.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine foundational definitions of intervals in an ordered set, with a vacuous axiom. Historically mildly interesting as a trace of the 1986 attempt to axiomatise tame/combinatorial topology from order-theoretic 'lines', but there is no new mathematics on this page.
transcription_corrections: The crossed-out heading reads approximately 'Définition Segments, intervalles, demi-intervalles (cas d'une structure de réseau)'. It is struck through, with 'tronçons' written above as the replacement.
The marginal NB likely reads 'NB les conditions a), b), c) sont satisfaites si cardinal ≤ 1 !' It justifies adding axiom d) card L > 1.
In a) the inequality 'L_{>a} ≠ ∅' appears to be kept (the stroke is over an earlier attempt), i.e. 'tel que L_{>a} ≠ ∅, L_{>a} est filtrant décroissant'.
'Position modifiée' / 'Modf' (previous and next pages) may possibly be 'modérée' (tame), which fits the context of 'topologie modérée'; this is uncertain from the handwriting.
